display_title: Official Review of Paper3539 by Reviewer HGnR

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new approach for learning on dynamic graphs, which avoids the need of convolution for aggregating information from past interactions by maintaining a summary (of the interactions) that is updated in an online fashion with a fixed and scalable aggregation process (i.e. a weighted average based on a softmax kernel that decays linearly wrt the number of events). Thanks to the recursive formulation that the selected aggregation process admits (which allows to update the summary of a node’s neighborhood whenever this is involved in a new event), the proposed approach shows a O(1) complexity both in terms of memory and number of operations for each update and inference step. Experimental evaluations on Reddit, Wikipedia, MOOC and Twitter dataset for link prediction and Wikipedia and Reddit for node classification show the good performance of the proposed solution, which performs on par with previous approaches in most of the considered scenarios (and in some even better) while requiring a fraction of the computational cost.
content.main_review:
Overall the paper is rather well written, it is easy to follow and the main idea is clear and generally well explained. While the paper achieves good performance on the considered tasks, I believe the authors slightly misunderstood the formulation of TGN and proposed in their paper a simplified version of that architecture, which however ends up performing better than what presented in Rossi et al. Indeed, at the end of section 2 the authors state:

In the l-th SAMPLE function, TGN selects the last n nodes that have interacted with the leaves of the graph G_u^{(l-1)}. Subsequently, TGN encodes the timestamps with random Fourier features (Rahimi & Recht, 2008) and uses temporal graph attention for AGGREGATE. The output of the last aggregation layer is a single node, and READOUT returns its feature vector. Finally, TGN uses the identity function for COMBINE and a GRU for UPDATE.

However, TGN doesn’t use any graph convolutional layer for determining the update of the memory cell, rather it exchanges messages across nodes that are involved in each interaction and updates the memory cell of each node based on an aggregated version of these messages (similarly to what is done in the paper with the computation of the summary of the neighbors state, just aggregating the messages that appear only in the last batch instead of the entire past history of a node). A graph convolutional layer is used only on top of these cells during inference to avoid the stainless of the memory and make a prediction for each node based on the latest state of the neighborhood (which might have evolved indeed from the last time the target node u was involved in an interaction - e.g. if a neighbor was interacting with a node different then u) - see Section 3.1 embedding of TGN’s paper for reference.

From this perspective the approach proposed by the authors appears as a simplified version of TGN where:

1) The GRU is replaced with the attention kernel proposed in the paper (the node state s and neighbrohood summary r can be considered as an analogous version of the GRU memory cells in this scenario, where the process for updating r is fixed by the attention kernel instead of being learnt by the GRU)

2) The graph convolutional layer applied on top of the memory cells for producing the output is simply replaced by a MLP (which would correspond to the identity embedding presented in TGN).

While the contribution of the paper appears thus incremental wrt what already proposed in TGN, I believe the approach is generally interesting and corresponds to a simple yet effective architecture for inference on dynamic graphs. The experiments show in this sense good performance wrt prior art and highlight whether some components (e.g. the graph convolutional layers realized in TGN or the attention layer used in TGAT) might actually not be needed for achieving good performance at least on the considered datasets. 

Overall, I would thus consider the paper a weak accept for ICLR and I would kindly ask the authors to reply to my points on the comparison with TGN in their rebuttal and if agreeing with me on the comparison to adjust the text of the paper to reflect the real contribution of the manuscript wrt prior art.
content.summary_of_the_review: While not presenting significant technical novelty, the paper presents some interesting insights for realizing a simple yet scalable architecture for inference on dynamic graphs. Experimental evaluation of the paper is overall sound and highlights well the benefit of the approach. The text needs refactoring to highlight the real contribution of the paper wrt prior art.

display_title: Response to Reviewer HGnR: Relationship between OGN and TGN

content.title: Response to Reviewer HGnR: Relationship between OGN and TGN
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedback. You brought up an important question regarding the connection between OGN and TGN that allows us to highlight the novelty of our paper. We hope that our answers have addressed your concerns and, if so, we kindly ask you to consider increasing your score. 

**"I believe the authors slightly misunderstood the formulation of TGN .... TGN doesn’t use any graph convolutional layer for determining the update of the memory cell (...)".** We believe that our exposition of TGNs might have been confusing. As you pointed out, TGNs do not apply graph convolutional layers to update node states in the memory block. We convey this idea in Equation 5 --- the update of the state vector does not depend on the output of the graph convolution layer (denoted by $h_{u}$ in our paper). In fact, the update only depends on the states of the interacting nodes, the edge information, and the timestamp. We believe the confusion stems from our effort to introduce a rather general formulation that accommodates both TGN and CAW. We will sharpen our description of T-GNNs and update the paragraph at the end of Section 2 (TGN) in the revised manuscript.

**"From this perspective the approach proposed by the authors appears as a simplified version of TGN".** Thanks for bringing up this issue. Importantly, the connection between TGN and OGN is not as straightforward as one may initially think. For instance, we can easily build a proof-like argument to show that OGN does not correspond to a simplified version of TGN using identity embedding module, as suggested here: 


> "...which would correspond to the identity embedding presented in TGN."

_Sketch of the proof:_ Let us assume an identity embedding module for TGN. To predict an event between nodes $i$ and $j$ with edge features $e_{ij}$, the node states $s_i$ and $s_j$ used for prediction do not depend on the interaction feature $e_{ij}$, but only on the information of previous events. In other words, TGN uses the features of the predicted events only in its embedding module. Please, see Figure 2 of Rossi et al. (2020) and note that information regarding novel events -- with timestamps $t_5$ and $t_6$ -- only appear in the embedding module. In contrast, the node states used for prediction in OGN are a function of $e_{ij}$. Therefore, OGN cannot be cast into a corresponding TGN with identity embedding.

Even if we considered other embedding modules (e.g., mixing state with edge and time information), we could not fit OGN in the framework. This is because the embedding TGN uses for prediction differs from its updated node state, whereas the embedding that OGN uses for prediction equals the updated node state.


In the following paragraphs, we further entertain two attempts at reducing OGN to TGN and show how they fail.

_Attempt 1._ Under a non-identity embedding module, an option to cast OGN into the TGN framework would be to treat the aggregated message of TGN (Equation 3, Rossi et al. (2020)) as the neighborhood state of OGN $r$. However, the aggregated message for TGN only depends on the messages in the batch, and cannot capture the complete history of interaction as the neighborhood state of OGN does. Thus, fitting OGN into TGN in this way would require extending the aggregated message in TGN to consider the complete history of messages for a node. Note that this not only changes the framework proposed in Rossi et al. (2020), but would also result in a model that increases both computational and memory complexity with respect to OGN.

_Attempt 2._ Another reduction attempt would be to extend TGN to include the neighborhood state as a memory cell. However, this would require extending the memory cell and its update in TGN, which we argue would defeat the purpose of calling OGN a simplification of TGN.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3539 by Reviewer oULy

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes Online Graph Network, a graph neural network for fast learning on temporal graphs.
The proposed method aims to overcome the computational burden of performing neighbor sampling and message passing whenever a prediction for a node is required. Instead, the authors propose a novel way to aggregate efficiently the neighbor representations continuously in an online manner. The idea is to keep a constant latent representation for the neighborhood of each node by adding to it the temporal representation of each neighbor that takes part in any past event. This means that the representations are updated in constant time as the events progress. The addition of a neighbor's representation is weighted based on an exponential decay term that is reversely analogous to the time between the current representation and the time of the neighbor's event.
Empirical results on four well-known datasets are performed to show the superiority in accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach compared with previous methods for link prediction, and two datasets for node classification.
content.main_review:
Pros: 

+ The motivation to increase the scalability and efficiency of temporal graphs is clear, as many real-world temporal graphs are very large. 

+ The idea is straight forward, which renders its adaptation easier and more interpretable for real world applications.

+ The experimental section and the ablation studies are well written and sufficiently explanatory.


Cons: 
- Since the main task of the model is to focus on the efficiency for real world applications, there should be a comparison for the inference time as well. Training time is indeed helpful but it is typically run once every certain period. Inference time is of equal importance in real applications that call for fast predictions. That would clarify the benefit of OGN over other baselines. Ideally, the model would benefit by running experiments with actual large graphs, as the largest right now is only 11000 nodes, however, I understand that due to the lack of such datasets this might be a hard argument to form.

- The paper could greatly benefit from expanding the experimental part. The section for node classification relies solely on two datasets, which lack node attributes and the advantages of OGN are not clear. To justify the use of OGN in this context, the authors could compare with numerous methods and datasets from the literature of temporal graph learning that can be found in the literature [1,2,3]. If OGN is useful specifically for interaction prediction on temporal graphs with no node attributes and edge attributes, it should be stated in the abstract.

[1] Diffusion convolutional recurrent neural network: Data-driven traffic forecasting
[2] PyTorch Geometric Temporal: Spatiotemporal Signal Processing with Neural Machine Learning Models
[3] GEM: A Python Package for Graph Embedding Methods

- As another attempt to increase the overall body of work,  the authors could expand the methods traditionally used for evaluation of interaction prediction in previous approaches such as Rossi et al. 2020.  To my understanding the model is evaluated by predicting the probability of an edge at a given time and contrast it with the probability of a random edge. Given that the random edge might be very hard to actually exist, there are certain easy heuristics that can be used as baselines, for example, predict the edge with the highest number of common neighbors or common neighbors in the past t events.  Alternatively, one could draw a negative edge between nodes that actually have edges but in previous or future time steps, instead of totally random.

-The included code contains instructions for wikipedia and reddit but not for the rest of the data. 


Comments: 
* Regarding notations, in equations 1-3 it is not clear whether the L samplings are performed before the first aggregation layer or each sampling is performed right before the respective aggregation layer. 

* Figure 2 could benefit from depicting the computation of \hat{G} along with the already present G.

*It is not clear whether there is an argument against the use of the original timestamps. Specifically the authors rely solely on the order of the events or U-time, a uniform time difference. However the time difference between events can be important i.e. if the difference between two events is 1 week or 1 month, we would expect the prediction to be affected since it relies on aggregating the past events. If this is not the case it could be an interesting observation and should be clarified.

*Is it possible to connect the proposed methodology with any theoretical findings from the literature of streaming algorithms?
content.summary_of_the_review: As the authors contend in the introduction the proposed method, though insightful, is quite simple, meaning that it has to indicate either a significant advantage over extended experiments or some theoretical justification, in order to not be considered a marginal contribution. The experiments indicate an acceleration in 3 out of 4 datasets and an improvement in precision in (different) 3 out of 4. The existence of edge features (as noted in the limitations) is catalytic, as the appendix experiments indicate that OGN performs worse than the benchmark in 3 datasets without edge features. With that in mind, I have the above comments to further justify OGN.

content.title: Response to Reviewer oULy
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful feedback. You suggested interesting additional experiments which we have conducted to strengthen our paper. More specifically, we have added new results regarding inference time and the performance under a different sampling scheme. We hope that our answers have clarified the issues you raised. In this case, we kindly ask you to consider increasing your score. 

**"there should be a comparison for the inference time as well".** Thank you for the suggestion. The table below reports results regarding inference time, using batch-size 30 in the test set. Notably, OGN is the fastest method overall. We will include this table in the revised version of our paper.

**Table 1: Inference time (seconds) in the transductive setting.**

| Model | Reddit | Wikipedia |  MOOC | Twitter |
|:-----:|:------:|:---------:|:-----:|:-------:|
|  TGAT |   420  |    687    |  246  |  1,064  |
|  TGN  |   132  |    182    |   88  |    98   |
|  CAW  |  2,218 |   2,068   | 1,337 |  1,494  |
|  OGN  |   **35**   |     **5**     |   **12**  |    **24**   |

**"the model would benefit by running experiments with actual large graphs".** We agree that using larger datasets would be beneficial to our method. However, as you pointed out, there is a lack of really large benchmarks for continuous-time dynamic graphs. In our work, we employ the largest datasets available in the literature.

**"authors could compare with numerous methods and datasets from the literature of temporal graph learning...[1,2,3]".**  Thank you for the suggestion. However, note that the pointers you provided focus on spatio-temporal forecasting and this evaluation setup cannot be easily extended to methods like CAW, TGN, TGAT, and OGN (ours). Graph representation is the major issue here. In our setup, temporal graphs are represented only as a series of interactions between nodes. Notably, we cover most of the datasets that apply to our setting (i.e., those in the TGAT, CAW, JODIE, and TGN papers).

**"...one could draw a negative edge between nodes that actually have edges but in previous or future time steps, instead of totally random."** Thank you for the insightful comment. We trained and evaluated the models in a new setting. For a node $u$, the negative edges consider only its temporal neighbors. For all models, we use the same hyperparameters as in the original setting. In this case, the results are expected to be worse than those with the original sampling, as the task is harder. We present the results in the Table below. OGN achieves the best performance in two datasets (Reddit and MOOC). We will include these results in the supplementary material.

**Table 2: Results (AP) using negative sampling on visited nodes in the transductive setting.**

| Model | Reddit | Wikipedia | MOOC |
|:-----:|:------:|:---------:|:----:|
|  TGAT |  66.7  |    60.8   | 63.8 |
|  TGN  |  _95.6_  |    **97.7**   | 78.5 |
|  CAW  |  63.9  |    67.9   | _82.3_ |
|  OGN  |  **97.6**  |    _94.5_   | **91.1** |

**"The included code contains instructions for wikipedia and reddit but not for the rest of the data."** We will include instructions for the other datasets when publishing our code in a repository.

**"in equations 1-3 it is not clear whether the L samplings are performed before the first aggregation layer or each sampling is performed right before the respective aggregation layer."** The sampling step in Equation 1 is performed $L$ times before the first aggregation layer.

**"Figure 2 could benefit from depicting the computation of \hat{G} along with the already present G."** Thank you for pointing this out.  We will improve Figure 2 in the updated version of our paper.

**"It is not clear whether there is an argument against the use of the original timestamps."** Subsection 6.1 (Figure 5a) shows that using discretized timestamps generally does not harm performance. Moreover, discrete timestamps can even improve the model performance in many cases. This result highlights that fine-grained timestamps are not crucial for the model's performance. In other words, there is evidence that using discretized timestamps leads to performance gain. Other than that, we do not have a strong claim against the use of original timestamps.

**"Is it possible to connect the proposed methodology with any theoretical findings from the literature of streaming algorithms?"** In our paper, we refer to OGN as a streaming algorithm due to its constant requirement of memory to process each interaction (the event information and the nodes involved in the interaction), without the need to access older events in history, in contrast to previous T-GNNs. However, we are not aware of related developments in the algorithms community.

content.title: Answer to your remaining concerns
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

We are glad you were pleased with our additional results. Nonetheless, we would like to briefly answer your remaining concerns.

**Relationship to other methods. OGN is far from a small variation of something in the literature.** Please see our answer to Reviewer HGnR, who raised a similar point. In our rebuttal, we show OGN does not fit in the general framework by Rossi et al. (2020). 

**"narrowness of the method's applicability ... compared to spatiotemporal problems".** To the best of our knowledge, spatiotemporal methods are not more general than OGN (or CAW, TGN, and TGAT) and cannot solve dynamic link prediction in CTDGs. 

**Lack of theory.** Note that none of the previous works we compare against show theoretical guarantees. Nonetheless, developing a theory for T-GNNs is an important open problem, that merits a work on its own. To the best of our knowledge, the first preliminary work (Gao and Ribeiro, 2021) in this direction has been recently released in ArXiv. 

J. Gao, B. Ribeiro. On the Equivalence Between Temporal and Static Graph Representations for Observational Predictions: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07016

display_title: Official Review of Paper3539 by Reviewer 5rxL

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers inference tasks over graphs, where the graph is dynamically evolving with time. The evolution happens in small increments where at each increment event either an edge is added or removed from the graph (though much of the discussion in the paper seems to be focused on only edge addition events). Under this setting it proposes an online graph net architecture, by which a node’s state is dynamically updated each time an edge event involving the node occurs. A key contribution in this architecture is the lack of neighborhood sampling for updating node states. It instead proposes using a hidden node state that effectively holds a summary of all updates involving the node that have occurred thus far, with preference given to recent events. As a result, the proposed method is much faster compared to baseline while providing comparable empirical performance.
content.main_review:
The paper is reasonably well-written, addresses an interesting problem, and proposes a simple and effective solution. I enjoyed reading it. However, I found there are some important aspects that have been omitted in the exposition. 
- It is easy to see that OGNs would be faster compared to baselines that consider neighborhood information for making predictions. However (as has been noted in Section 6.2), OGNs risk not using graph structural information which might be harmful for certain problems. For e.g., if an edge event (u, v) happens, while r_u and r_v are updated, the states of the 2-hop and 3-hop neighbors of u, v are not updated. Moreover, if during prediction time only the local states s_u, s_v are used then it the graph information is not being used at all. It is surprising how the method is able to perform competitively given this potentially serious drawback. Are the choice of experiments such that the graph information is not that useful for predictions? 
- A discussion on how OGNs are trained (and backpropagated) is missing. For instance, it is unclear whether each training sample corresponds to a distinct temporal sequence of edge additions starting from an initial graph, or whether training can be performed “online” over a single (long) sequence of edge additions/removals. In Fig. 4 does time refer to training time or testing time?  
- How are edge removals handled by OGN? How are node additions/removal handled? 
- In Equation 5, the righthand side does not have h_u(t). Is this a typo? 
- Equation 6 is designed in a way that older events are forgotten compared to recent events. However, for some applications an old event might contain information that is relevant long after the event has happened. How does OGN deal with such cases? Have you considered using a GRU (for example) to update r_u?
content.summary_of_the_review: Reasonable well-written paper that proposes a simple, effective solution to learning over temporally changing graphs. Some crucial aspects are missing from the discussion. It would make the paper stronger, if those points are addressed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5rxL
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful feedback. We are updating our paper to reflect important issues raised in your review. In particular, we are $i$) highlighting that our approach can leverage various importance decay schemes, and $ii$) adding details regarding the training procedure. We hope our answers have sufficiently addressed your concerns, and if that is the case, we kindly ask you to consider increasing your score.

**"if during prediction time only the local states $s_u$, $s_v$ are used then the graph information is not being used at all''**

During prediction, we incorporate the target edge $(e, t)$ and neighborhood information $r_u$ to compute $s_u$. We understand it might seem like $r_u$ only carries information of immediate neighbors, but this is not the case. In fact, we use an inductive argument to prove exactly the opposite (please, see our answer to Reviewer HSHM). We reproduce the argument below.

_OGN does exploit multi-hop structural information_. More specifically, when we update node $u$'s neighborhood state $r_{u}$ upon interaction $(u, v)$, we factor in $v$'s state $s_v$. In turn, $s_v$ depends on $v$'s neighborhood. Using transitivity, this argument can be extended to show $r_{u}$ depends on all nodes in temporal walks terminating at $u$.

**"Are the choice of experiments such that the graph information is not that useful for predictions?"**
 
We validate OGN using virtually all public benchmarks (attributed or not) from previous works attacking the same problem (TGN, TGAT, and CAW). Also, note that our evaluation is more comprehensive than that in the TGN and TGAT papers, which only consider attributed datasets. Therefore, we have made our best effort to ensure a fair assessment of our method. Nonetheless, if the reviewer is correct, it implies a severe issue with the evaluation protocol of previous works, and exploring it merits an investigation of its own.

**"A discussion on how OGNs are trained (and backpropagated) is missing".**

Thanks for pointing this out. For training, we follow the setting of previous T-GNNs for continuous-time dynamic graphs (e.g., TGN, TGAT, and CAW). Recall that the dataset is a long sequence of events. Then, we partition these events into non-overlapping batches that are contiguous in time. At each epoch, our method goes over all batches in chronological order. Also, at the beginning of each epoch, we reset the memory (node states) and the neighborhood information. We will add details regarding the training procedure (including backpropagation) to our revised manuscript.

**"In Fig. 4 does time refer to training time or testing time?"** 

The values reported in Figure 4 correspond to training time, as it refers to time _per epoch_. We will clarify this in the caption. We will also include a comparison for the inference time in the updated version of the manuscript.

**"How are edge removals handled by OGN? How are node additions/removal handled?"**

In principle, there are some ways in which deletion events could be treated. One possibility is to treat them as regular events with an additional feature/flag that indicates deletion. Regarding node deletion, we could also remove its state from the model. Because of OGN's exponentially decaying weights, deleting a node's state will naturally remove the node's effect (on other node representations) over time. Nonetheless, given the lack of proper benchmarks, current T-GNNs cannot validate strategies for deletion events. For further discussion, please see the answer to Reviewer HSHM.

**"In Equation 5, the righthand side does not have $h_u(t)$. Is this a typo?"** 

No. The node embedding $h_u$ is not involved in the recursive state update in Equation 5. T-GNNs only use the output embedding $h_u$ for prediction purposes. 

**"... an old event might contain information that is relevant long after the event has happened. How does OGN deal with such cases?"** 

The most straightforward way is to decrease the temperature scaling -- i.e., make $\alpha$ approach zero in Equation 6. When we do so, old events remain important indeterminately. However, OGN is also compatible with arbitrary weighting schemes. As mentioned in our answer to Reviewer HSHM, it suffices to change $\exp{(-\alpha m)}$ by your desired weighting function. We will add a remark to the updated version of our paper regarding the weighting scheme. 

**"Have you considered using a GRU (for example) to update $r_u$?"**

Thanks for your suggestion. In principle, using a GRU might help the model learn different forgetting rates. However, we chose a simpler updating scheme to make our model faster. Nonetheless, we think leveraging adaptive weighting schemes (e.g., GRU) is a good direction for future investigation and will mention it in the discussion.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3539 by Reviewer HSHM

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on learning node representations for continuous-time dynamic graphs. The overall approach follows the setup in recently proposed works where the state of nodes involved in an event are updated after each event and most recent node states (representations) are used for prediction and classification tasks. The node representations are updated using its previous state, features of the edge representing the event, random Fourier temporal features and its temporal neighborhood information. The key contribution of this paper is the proposal a simpler computation of the neighborhood information in an online manner for replacing the more expensive attention and message passing based techniques used in previous works. To achieve this, the proposed technique maintains two variables a_u and b_u, that account for the most recent summary of neighborhood information, decayed linearly with respect to the number of events. The authors demonstrate substantial training speedup over several state-of-art methods and also showcase slightly better or comparable performance to representative baselines for the task of link prediction and node classification.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

- The technique proposed to compute the neighborhood representation online is simple and intuitive.
- The speedup advantage during training is substantial and noticeable.
- The experiments are performed across variety of datasets and compared to state-of-art baselines along with various ablations which is a strong point of the paper.

Weaknesses:

- The overall approach and setup is not novel and follows various recent works sighted by the authors which makes the key contribution on the method to update neighborhood crucial. While the technique does produce speedup, it may not be generalizable to different domains. For instance, the approach assumes that importance decay of each neighbor is linear in terms of number of events on that node however, this may not be true in many cases. For instance, many edge types may have longer effect (e.g. share) vs others (e.g. like). In this scenario, the current approach would fail to correctly weight the neighbors. 
- Further, the key benefit of using message passing scheme is to use the structural information effectively and as shown by authors own experiments on graphs with no edge information, the approach does not effectively account for structural information which limits its applicability.
- If I understand correctly, proposition 1 only holds in case linear decay and hence the approach cannot be easily extended to nonlinear temporal dependencies. Related to that, the ablation study on time information is not clear to me. The results for no time vs original time are quite mixed and it is not clear why authors conclude that this means the only required information from time is order of events.
- Authors talk about node addition and deletion being represented as event. However, it doesn’t seem like the approach can handle node deletion. Deleting a node should have effect on its previous neighbors but there is no way to handle this in the current approach.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach is a useful update to  the already existing frameworks for learning representations over dynamic graphs and will be of interest to practitioners. However, the overall contribution of the paper is weak and also the key contribution of removing the bottleneck on computing neighborhood representation may have severe limitations when it comes to graphs with no edge features or graphs where dependence on events may not decay linearly over time as described above. Hence I believe this contribution is marginally below the acceptance threshold.

content.title: Response to Reviewer HSHM
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback. Based on your review, we are updating our paper to highlight how our approach can leverage various importance weighting schemes and exploit multi-hop structural information. If our answers have sufficiently addressed your concerns, we kindly ask you to consider raising your score.

**"The overall approach and setup is not novel"**

While our contribution might be simple, we believe that it is significantly novel and produces huge speed-ups compared to the previous art. Notably, the main mechanism in our method (i.e., using an auxiliary variable to store neighborhood information) is original and has never appeared in previous works. 
OGN's mechanism is not only an efficient alternative to temporal message-passing, but also holds the promise of T-GNNs for (truly) web-scale applications (as discussed in Section 3.2). We also believe that a simple method like OGN excelling in relevant benchmarks is a critical finding --- and perhaps an eye-opener for the community. 

**"as shown by authors ...[OGN] does not effectively account for structural information"**

We note that, on non-attributed datasets (Table 9, Supplement), OGN consistently outperforms TGAT and there is no clear winner between TGN and OGN. Only CAW is consistently better than OGN in non-attributed data. While CAW's anonymous walks seem to capture structural patterns in the graphs, CAW runs orders of magnitude slower. Furthermore, computing these walks requires repeated access to the main memory, which is a critical bottleneck for web-scale networks. 

We also want to clarify that **OGN does exploit multi-hop structural information**. More specifically, when we update node $u$'s neighborhood state $r_{u}$ upon interaction $(u, v)$, we factor in $v$'s state $s_v$. In turn, $s_v$ depends on $v$'s neighborhood. Using transitivity, this argument can be extended to show $r_{u}$ depends on all nodes in temporal walks terminating at $u$.

**"...importance decay of each neighbor is  [exponentially] linear ..., this may not be true in many cases".**

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree there might exist a scenario in which this decay is not ideal. However, this bias is included in previous literature (see CAW) and does not appear to be a hindrance in what concerns experimental results. This might also hint at the need for better benchmarks for temporal GNNs. Nonetheless, we can also adapt OGN to handle arbitrary weighting schemes (see the answer below). We will include this discussion as a remark in our revised manuscript.

**"Proposition 1 holds only for [exponentially] linear decay"**

While Proposition 1 is tied to this decay schedule via Eqs 7 and 8, is still valid for arbitrary weighting schemes. For implementation purposes, it suffices to change $\exp{(-\alpha m)}$ by your desired weighting function. We will add a remark in the updated version of our paper regarding the weighting scheme. 

**"The results for no time vs original time are quite mixed and it is not clear why authors conclude that this means the only required information from time is order of events."**

We agree with the reviewer that the results of No-time and original time are mixed. However, we do not claim that this implies that only the ordering matters. In fact, we state in Appendix D: "...these results show that there are cases in which leveraging the ordering of events alone is not enough to learn meaningful temporal node representations." Note that in the main paper we show that methods using $\mathcal{U}$-time (different from no-time explained in Appendix D) generally outperform their counterparts that use original time. From this, what we conclude is that fine-grained information is not crucial for T-GNNs (Section 6.1).

**"...it doesn’t seem like the approach can handle node deletion"**
To some extent, we agree. In fact, i) most of the previous related works do not present an in-depth discussion on the effects of deletion events both on the predictive models and the data structure/representation; and ii) none of the existing benchmarks comprise deletion events. The notable exception to the former is Rossi et al. (2020), that hypothesize about deletion events but show no experimental results. For instance, this inability to handle deletion events has been recently pointed out by Skarding et al. (arXiv:2005.07496; Table 6, pg 19).

Nonetheless, an option to deal with node deletions in OGN is to delete its states from the model. Because of OGN's exponentially decaying weights, deleting a node's state will naturally remove the node's effect (on other node representations) over time. Still, it is impossible to evaluate the validity of this strategy without proper baselines. 

J. Skarding et al. Foundations and Modeling of Dynamic Networks Using Dynamic Graph Neural Networks: A Survey. ArXiv:2005.07496, 2021.

E.  Rossi et al.   Temporal  graph networks for deep learning on dynamic graphs. ArXiv:2006.10637, 2020.

display_title: Comments from authors of CAW paper

content.title: Comments from authors of CAW paper
content.comment:
We are the authors of "Causal Anonymous Walk" (CAW), one of the major baselines with which this paper compares. We think this is a well-written paper that constitutes significant contributions to faster and better temporal graph learning by replacing temporal neighborhood extraction with well-designed event-based embedding update. Meanwhile, we would like to respectfully point out that **CAW is more accurate and faster** than its performance reported in this paper. It has also been brought to our attention that this paper reports an issue with CAW’s implementation. We would also like to seek this chance to respond and to provide more information. 

First, we highly appreciate the authors for pointing out an issue with our implementation of attention. We acknowledge the issue. We have fixed our code and have run experiments relevant to this paper. We are also working hard to update our paper to reflect any relevant correction. After fixing the issue, we found that it is better to set tolerance=1e-4 (or even 0) for the early stopping strategy. The previous default was 1e-3, which will now cause insufficient training.

The following discussions are all based on CAWN-attn with the correct implementation.

In Figure 1 of this paper, CAW’s performance is drawn at the right-bottom corner of the scatter plot. However, in our efforts to update our experiments, we found that CAW is faster and more accurate than reported:
1.	CAW’s transductive performance on Reddit is significantly higher than 98.0%, which is supported both by table 1 of this paper and by the updated experiments done by ourselves. This contradicts with Figure 1 which puts it below 98.0%.
2.	In this Figure 1, CAW’s training time per epoch is rated at 5 times that of TGAT, and 39 times TGN. However, we do not think this is fair comparison. We note that the default batch size of both TGAT and TGN is 200, whereas CAW uses 32 by default. Since we could not find it, we assume this is the setting used to generate Figure 1. If that is the case, then we think it is unfair to compare the epoch time because a larger batch size means shorter epoch time but slower gradient descent per epoch, so the tradeoff cannot be seen as an advantage. If Figure 1 is, instead, generated using equal batch size with other hyperparameters as default, then their epoch times are comparable but in that case the average wall clock time comparisons are the following (unit: min/epoch, bs=32): CAWN-attn: 102, CAWN-mean: 76, TGAT: 48, TGN: 23. While the numbers can slightly vary in practice, the magnitude of contrast deviates from what’s being shown.

Meanwhile, experiments show that CAW's performance on Reddit is higher than that reported by this paper’s Table 1. CAW's performance on Reddit and Wikipedia is also higher than that reported by this paper’s Table 5 (Appendix) which by the way seems not consistent with Table 1. More concretely, running our code at https://github.com/snap-stanford/CAW with commands attached to the end generates 98.78% (+-0.09%) on Reddit, and 98.71% (+-0.11%) on Wikipedia, both measured in AP under transductive setting. These numbers are higher than reported. 

Finally, and more importantly, it is our sincerest hope to avoid misunderstandings and to improve our published implementation of CAW to benefit more people. We understand that even the slightest difference in implementation can lead to significant difference in results. In that regard, we would be extremely appreciative if the authors could very kindly share the CAW code and commands used to generate their results in Table 1 and 8.

Authors of the Inductive Representation Learning in Temporal Networks via Causal Anonymous Walks


Reddit: python main.py -d reddit --pos_dim 108 --agg walk --bs 32 --n_degree 32 1 --mode t --bias 1e-5 --pos_enc lp --walk_pool attn --seed 0 --tolerance 1e-4

Wikipedia: python main.py -d wikipedia --pos_dim 108 --agg walk --bs 32 --n_degree 64 1 --mode t --bias 1e-6 --pos_enc lp --walk_pool attn --seed 0 --tolerance 1e-4

All experiments were run on a server configured with Xeon Gold 6148 2.4G Hz CPU and Nvidia 2080 Ti GPU.

replying_to: Replying to Comments from authors of CAW paper
display_title: Response to the authors of CAW

content.title: Response to the authors of CAW
content.comment:
Thank you for providing positive comments about our work, including that it constitutes significant contributions to faster and better temporal graph learning. Also, we are glad that you have validated our findings wrt the implementation issue of CAW. In the following paragraphs, we respond to your questions/comments. But before doing that, and to avoid possible misunderstandings, we note first that the **empirical findings regarding our method remain unshaken**:
 1. OGN is a very simple method that achieves competitive performance against SOTA T-GNNs on relevant benchmarks; 
 2. OGN is significantly faster than the existing T-GNNs, including CAW.

We now respond to your comments. Please, let us know if you have further questions.

**Regarding Figure 1.**  Thanks for catching the inconsistency between Figure 1 and Table 1. The former corresponds to an old version of our draft. We will fix the plot to match Table 1 in our revised manuscript. 

**Regarding the training time.** To ensure a fair comparison, we used batch-size 200 (default value in TGN) for all methods. We believe the difference between our values and the ones you have provided may come from differences in: 
   1. _Experimental setup_: We follow the same experimental setup as Rossi et al. (TGN, 2020), which slightly differs from the setup used to train CAW. In the transductive setting, Rossi et al. (2020) randomly select 10\% of the nodes and remove any link associated with them in the training set, whereas CAW uses the complete training set.
   2. _Batch size and hyper-parameters_: We used batch-size 200 and walks of length 3 (found via model selection), whereas you reported numbers with 32 and walks of length 2. 
   3. _Hardware_: We use a machine with an Intel Xeon E5-2630 2.2GHz CPU and an NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti 8Gb GPU, which again differs from what you used.

To analyze how the hyper-parameters impact the training time, we re-run our experiments with batch-size 32 and walk-length 2 on Reddit --- the same hyperparameters you used. We got 79 min/epoch for CAW-attn. Curiously, we achieved faster training than you reported (79 min/epoch vs. 102 min/epoch). We believe the remaining gap (that still amounts to $\approx$20\%) stems from differences in the experimental setup and computational resources.

We noticed that CAW's running time is very sensitive to the amount of available RAM. This is reasonable since CAW samples walks using the CPU and may require repeatedly accessing the main memory/disk. As an example, CAW's running time (per epoch) goes from 10 hours to 2 hours if we increase the RAM limit from 40GB to 50GB. We also noticed that under batch-size 32, the gap between OGN and CAW reduces (e.g., OGN takes 5 min/epoch vs. CAW 79 min/epoch). We will include this discussion and results with batch-size 32 in our revised paper.

**Regarding differences in AP.** In addition to the difference in setup and hyper-parameters, we believe the performance difference --- 98.78%  (ours: 98.39%) on Reddit, and 98.71% (ours: 98.63%) on Wikipedia, can come from the updated tolerance for early stopping. We used the original value 1e-3, whereas you now have reported values for 1e-4. We forgot to mention the tolerance for CAW in the Appendix but will do so in the revised manuscript.

Importantly, we highlight that our results rely on the official code released with the CAW paper but with the corrected attention layer. Nonetheless, we will accept your request and make our implementation available together with the revised manuscript as part of the supplementary material in a few days. 

It is in our best interest to make sure that the camera-ready version of our paper reflects the correct accuracy of CAW. We are open to adding pointers to the up-to-date version of CAW in our Appendix and coordinating with you (CAW authors) to ensure good science.
